title: Binary optimal control by trust-region steepest descent
contribution: A trust-region steepest-descent method that optimizes binary controls directly as measurable sets, using a gradient density from a signed-measure derivative, with a proof of finite termination at epsilon-stationarity under inexact gradients and steps, and ODE, PDE and topology-optimization proofs of concept.
problem_entry: Binary optimal control recast as min J(U) over measurable sets of an atomless measure space; existing routes (maximum principle, DP, moment relaxations, CIA, first-discretize MINLP) lack a set-space descent method; closest relative Cea et al. [10], made generic as a trust-region method in a metric space (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Derivative as a finite signed measure with Radon-Nikodym density g_U; trust region measured by mu of the symmetric difference, so the subproblem is solved by a sublevel set of g_U found by bisection; classical ratio-test trust-region loop kept unchanged (pp. 5-8, 23-26).
assumptions: Assumption 1 (bounded-variation vector measure, Frechet-differentiable outer functional, ||nu(D)|| <= C mu(D), atomless) p. 5; Lipschitz derivative over conv nu(Sigma) chosen for brevity over a geodesic argument pp. 8-9; ODE case C2, affine-in-w (via partial outer convexification), boundary distance p. 13-14; PDE case nested bounded-eccentricity meshes pp. 20-21.
proof_devices: Signed-measure derivative via chain rule and tail bounds for sigma-additivity (Lemma 2, pp. 6-7)
First-order Taylor expansion in set space o(mu(D)) (Thm. 1, p. 7) and quadratic remainder LC^2 mu(D)^2/2 (Lemma 3, pp. 8-9)
Sublevel-set averaging lemma using atomlessness (Lemma 4, pp. 10-11)
Necessary optimality g_U >= 0 a.e. by contradiction (Lemma 5, pp. 11-12); instationarity measure and suboptimality bound (p. 12)
Gronwall bounds and costate Lagrangian Taylor expansion for Frechet differentiability in L1 (Lemmas 6-8, Thm. 2, pp. 14-19); Hamiltonian link (p. 20)
Lebesgue differentiation on refining meshes to approximate g from DOF gradients (p. 22)
Near-optimal bisection step within delta*Delta (Lemma 9, pp. 25-26)

Standard trust-region finite-termination argument with radius threshold and uniform decrease (Thm. 3, pp. 26-28); hypothesis (10) printed with a plus sign in the extracted text (p. 26), apparently a slip
experiments: Three proof-of-concept problems without competitors: Poisson source inversion in FEniCS (187 its, 167.79 CPU s, refinement 85.1% per Table 1 vs 87% in text, p. 32); Lotka-Volterra via CVODES adjoint callbacks with a time weight m(t) (90 its, 16.72 s, pp. 35-36); topology optimization with weighted sum and capped radius, failure modes reported (26 its, 484.94 s, pp. 39-42).
positioning: Places itself among topology-optimization descent methods by object (sets not level sets) and step type (cumulative), absorbs the Competing Hamiltonian approach as a special case, cites the Acta Numerica MINLP survey as the discretize-first route (pp. 2-3, 20).
writing: Caveats stated in the contribution paragraph (no iterate convergence, p. 3); outline promises answers to criticisms (p. 3); repeated 'proof of concept' labelling and an explicit reason for no comparison (p. 42).
limits_future: No iterate convergence (p. 3), no constraints (p. 39), discretization error uncontrolled (p. 23), not competitive in topology optimization (p. 42); future: constrained and higher-order NLP theory in measure spaces, fast MIOC with ODE/PDE constraints (p. 42).

method_links.note: Trust-region globalization and its convergence proof carried into binary control; proofs transferred from conventional NLP; also fits Heuristic 5 and Heuristic 8 (function space first; B&B on fine meshes at extreme disadvantage).
Claims calibrated as proof of concept with losses reported, but no baseline is run at all because fair comparison is judged hard.
Gradient density extracted from an off-the-shelf integrator's adjoint callbacks (CVODES), inheriting its adaptive grid.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Metric mu(A delta B) on control sets and sublevel-set steps of a gradient density instead of relaxing integrality.

transferable: Globalize on a non-vector space by choosing a (pseudo)metric whose ball makes the linear-model subproblem easy (sublevel-set selection under mu(A delta B) <= Delta).

Inexact-gradient trust-region proof: gradient tolerance proportional to omega*eps*Delta_i/mu(Omega), stationarity test at (1-omega/3)eps, radius threshold for acceptance, uniform decrease per accepted step (Thm. 3, pp. 26-28).
Ask the subproblem for a step size within a range and refine only candidate cells until the range is reachable (pp. 24-25).
Weight the measure (m(t) = 1 + t_f - t) so early and late control switches have comparable effect (p. 35).
Report per-component CPU time to locate where a new method's cost sits (Table 1, p. 32).

quotes.text: We present our work with the caveat that we do not prove ultimate convergence of the control sequence and that we do not even guarantee that it is a Cauchy sequence.
Outside of the field of topology optimization, where similar methods already exist, it is generally difficult to design fair comparisons to other methods.

title: Modeling and solving cascading failures across interdependent infrastructure systems
contribution: A robust bilevel interdiction model of multistage cascading failures in interdependent infrastructure, an exact mixed-binary LP reformulation of the follower via LP duality plus McCormick envelopes made exact by dual integrality, and a strengthened Benders-type decomposition, tested on networks generated from anonymized Puerto Rico data.
problem_entry: Find the most severe contingencies when dependencies are known only between asset classes (uncertain arc weights) and prior optimization work focuses on power-grid followers (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Dualize the robust inner minimum, linearize the resulting bilinear dual-primal terms by McCormick envelopes that are exact because optimal duals are binary, then solve the bilevel problem by a Benders loop with precomputed damage coefficients and cuts strengthened by releasing one attacked asset at a time (pp. 6-11).
assumptions: Synchronized cascade stages (p. 4), linear service degradation (p. 6), stage-invariant polytope of arc weights (p. 5); experiments use +-10% boxes around inverse-square-distance weights and frequency-inverse importance weights (p. 13).
proof_devices: LP dualization of the robust inner min into the follower (Prop. 1, pp. 6-7)
Binary optimal duals from stationarity 1 - lambda - pi = 0 plus complementary slackness (Lemma 1, p. 8)
Case analysis showing McCormick exactness for binary lambda (Thm. 2, pp. 8-9); negative remark that continuous-lambda McCormick is not exact on some networks (p. 9)
Repeated master solution closes the gap (Lemma 2, pp. 11-12); finite termination by enumeration of leader solutions (Thm. 3, p. 12)
experiments: Julia/JuMP/Gurobi 9.5.1, 1 h limit, 1% gap, networks a128 and a210 (pp. 13-14); (P_mc) gives identical optima and attack sets to (P_nl), 68.17% faster (Table 4, p. 14); Benders-S fewer iterations but loses on easy instances (p. 16); scalability over Np and Nc with gaps up to 55% at Np=4 (Tables 5-6, pp. 17-18); instance analyses (pp. 18-20); Tang et al. baseline run and fails (pp. 20-21).
positioning: Surveys non-optimization cascade studies and Stackelberg power-grid work, rejects single-level reformulation for size, concedes similarity of plain Benders to Salmeron-Wood and claims novelty for the strengthened cut (pp. 2-4, 20-21).
writing: Named formulations compared head to head; negative observations (non-exact continuous McCormick, Benders-S losing on easy instances) written into the text (pp. 9, 16).
limits_future: Time-limit gaps on hard instances (Table 5, p. 17), termination guaranteed only by enumeration (p. 12), synthetic networks (p. 13); future: stronger cuts, valid inequalities, symmetry (p. 21).

method_links.note: Bilinear follower reformulated to an exact MILP before changing the algorithm; both formulations kept and compared on the same solver.
Same-solver rule, stated gap and time limit, variant reported to lose on easy instances, literature baseline run and reported to fail.
Exactness bounded by observed counterexample networks for continuous lambda; hypothesis (binary lambda) made explicit.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: McCormick envelopes of dual-times-primal terms proved exact because the optimal duals are 0/1, then the binary restriction is imposed explicitly.

transferable: Dualize a robust max-with-zero constraint into the outer max; if duals are provably 0/1, linearize dual-primal products exactly by McCormick with binary duals (pp. 6-9).
Interdiction Benders: precompute per-asset damage bounds by a stage recursion over the dependency graph; strengthen each cut by re-solving with one attacked asset released (pp. 10-11).
Validate an exactness theorem by solving both formulations with the same solver and reporting identical optima (Table 4, p. 14).
Plot upper and lower bound trajectories to separate finding from proving optimality (Figs. 1-3, p. 15).
coauthors: Yijiang Li (first), Kibaek Kim, Matt Menickelly, Lawrence Paul Lewis, Joshua Bergerson

quotes.text: This set of results empirically confirms the exactness proof in Theorem 2.
This observation suggests that the optimal solution and objective values are likely to be found early in the execution of the algorithm, while proving optimality is a much more challenging task.

title: Heuristic algorithms for placing geomagnetically induced current blocking devices
contribution: A reformulated MINLP for GIC blocking-device placement (rectangular AC power flow, complementarity form of absolute values) and a three-block ADMM heuristic with a closed-form binary block, compared with a stochastic-learning heuristic and with SCIP and Juniper on EPRI-21 and UIUC-150 (read as the arXiv:2310.09409v1 PSCC 2024 manuscript).
problem_entry: Spatial B&B on the GIC-BDP MINLP is slow because of binaries, absolute-value equations and polar trigonometric trilinear terms (p. 1).
key_idea: Repair the formulation first (rectangular form, abs value as smooth complementarity), then split by consensus copies into a binary block solved greedily in closed form plus DC and AC NLP blocks (3ADMM-B) (pp. 2-4).
assumptions: Model (AC-rect) eqs. (1)-(10) (pp. 2-3); E-field direction fixed at 45 degrees and four magnitudes (p. 5); no convergence assumptions, the methods are heuristics (pp. 1, 3).
proof_devices: Binary identity ||z||^2 = <1,z> turning the binary ADMM block into a sorted greedy knapsack (Remark 1, p. 4)
Normalized primal/dual residual stopping rule (p. 4); no convergence theorem (n/a)
experiments: EPRI-21 (V=3) and UIUC-150 (V=30), E in {5,10,15,20} V/km; SCIP and Juniper with 1 h limit; all solutions evaluated by fixing binaries and solving the NLP (p. 5); SCIP gaps large (Fig. 4, pp. 5-6); heuristics give lower objective, 3ADMM-B < 100 s, SL < 1000 s (Fig. 5, p. 6); NRB 73 -> 19 iterations (p. 6); SL sample-size study (pp. 6-7); no repeated SL runs or solver settings reported.
positioning: Builds on the group's prior GMD work and Liang et al. branch-and-cut, departs from polar-form models, cites complementarity literature including Fletcher-Leyffer for the reformulation (pp. 1-3).
writing: Numbered contributions; strong claims of superior quality and speed vs state-of-the-art MINLP solvers based on single 1 h runs (pp. 1-2, 6).
limits_future: Only tuning of N discussed as a limit (p. 7); future: two-stage blocker placement plus line switching and ML-pretrained real-time recommendations (p. 7).

method_links.note: Abs value replaced by smooth complementarity (citing the MPEC-as-NLP line) and polar by rectangular power flow, justified by solver failure and instability.
MPEC reformulation and augmented-Lagrangian/ADMM splitting carried into a power-grid MINLP application.
Outperformance claim over SCIP and Juniper rests on 1 h default-like runs, single runs of a stochastic method and no class-wise rule of thumb; only the common evaluation meter is fair.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Integer vector duplicated into a binary block with a closed-form greedy solution and a relaxed continuous block linked by ADMM consensus.

transferable: Replace |Theta| by s+ - s- = Theta, |Theta| = s+ + s-, s+- >= 0, s+ s- <= 0 to avoid nonsmooth kinks in NLP-based MINLP solvers (eq. (10), p. 3).
In ADMM with binaries and a cardinality budget, the binary block becomes a sorted greedy because ||z||^2 = sum z (Remark 1, p. 4).
Evaluate heuristics and exact solvers on one meter: fix each method's binaries and solve the remaining NLP (p. 5).
Adapt the ADMM penalty by normalized residual balancing and report the iteration savings (eq. (23), Fig. 6, p. 6).
coauthors: Minseok Ryu (first), Ahmed Attia, Arthur Barnes, Russell Bent, Adam Mate

quotes.text: The absolute value in Eq. (8) is nonsmooth, which can cause convergence failure in MINLP solvers.
In contrast, we apply ADMM to a discrete optimization problem.

title: A bilevel optimization framework for imbalanced data classification
contribution: MUBO, a majority-undersampling algorithm whose accept/reject rule is motivated by a bilevel model (upper level: majority loss over majority subsets; lower level: training loss), with a lemma linking correct majority classification to lower majority loss and UCI results that beat SMOTE and GAN baselines on three of five datasets.
problem_entry: Oversampling adds noise and overlap through synthetic data and random undersampling under-fits; reject real majority points that do not reduce majority loss, as GANs reject synthetic points (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Bilevel model min over majority subsets of majority loss at trained weights; solved heuristically by drawing micro-samples, retraining, and accepting only those that do not increase majority loss (pp. 6-7).
assumptions: Softmax on scalar network output with binary cross-entropy (pp. 4-5); inner problem solved approximately by Adam to a gradient tolerance or epoch cap (pp. 7, 9); Definition 5 sums the false-majority loss over S_m in the extracted text, apparently a typo (p. 5).
proof_devices: Lemma 1: correct majority classification iff p(y=0|x) >= 1/2 iff loss <= log 2, hence loss of correctly classified points is below that of misclassified ones (p. 8); converse acknowledged to need extra conditions (p. 8)
experiments: Five UCI datasets, 20% test, five seeded runs, baseline-aligned architecture (pp. 9-10); SMOTified-GAN numbers taken from publication (p. 9); MUBO best F1 on Gisette, Abalone, Connect4 and worst on Ionosphere (Table 1, p. 9); minority/majority breakdown vs GBO (Table 3, p. 10); imbalance-ratio range in text inconsistent with Table 2 (pp. 9-10); code public (p. 9).
positioning: Data rebalancing vs model reweighting; long review of SMOTE and GAN hybrids; bilevel relatives AutoBalance and NAS share the lower level, novelty placed in the upper level (pp. 3-4).
writing: ATLAS motivation (p. 1); abstract's 'up to 10% higher' F1 is the most favourable pairwise gap while the text says next best is 1-2% lower (pp. 1, 9-10); Ionosphere loss explained (p. 10).
limits_future: Small datasets hinder the method (p. 10); additional conditions needed to link majority loss to F1 (p. 11); future: provable conditions and small-data performance (p. 11).

method_links.note: Bilevel leader-follower frame carried into ML data selection, but only the frame travels, not the NLP machinery; weak evidence.
Failures reported, seeds repeated, code public; but one baseline copied from publication and the abstract uses the most favourable gap.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A bilevel model is written to justify a greedy accept/reject heuristic rather than solved; the guarantee gap is acknowledged.

transferable: Data subset selection: accept a random micro-batch only if the target-class loss does not increase after retraining, and shrink the micro-batch once the accepted set passes a threshold (Alg. 1, p. 7).
Report minority and majority F1, precision and recall separately next to the averages (Table 3, p. 10).

quotes.text: Given that our method utilizes all available minority data, Ionosphere’s experimental results indicate that a small dataset size is a hindrance to our undersampling approach.
Additional conditions are required to formally prove experimental results showing improved majority loss implies improved average F1 score.

title: Population balance model-based dynamic multiobjective optimization of yeast cell manufacturing
contribution: A numerical-feasibility study of multiobjective optimal control for an oscillatory population-balance model of continuous yeast manufacturing: a discretization study, control vector parameterization with coarse-to-fine warm starts, weighted-sum Pareto sweeps via SLSQP, and tradeoff ratios between oscillatory and non-oscillatory Pareto policies.
problem_entry: No optimal-control study had explored Pareto tradeoffs between tolerated process oscillation (from Hopf bifurcations) and economic profit; prior work used linear MPC and input-output linearization (pp. 2, 4).
key_idea: Method-of-lines with WENO FDM chosen by an open-loop shoot-out, piecewise-linear CVP, weighted-sum objectives with input-smoothness regularization, and continuation from K to 2K control elements with multistarts (pp. 4-7).
assumptions: Idealized reactor (single substrate, constant volume, negligible gas phase) (p. 3); S' unobservable (p. 4); nondimensionalized variables, CFL bound nu_max = 1, stiff BDF integration (pp. 4-5); near-perfect model (p. 7).
proof_devices: CFL step bound and SSP/TVD properties of the time integrator (pp. 4-5, footnote 3)
Continuity of gradients under the regularized formulation (p. 6)
Epsilon-constraint verification of selected Pareto points, implementation not shown (p. 7)
Tradeoff ratios Lambda_{n,m} between two Pareto policies (eqs. (26)-(29), p. 7); no theorems (n/a)
experiments: Discretization shoot-out with wall times (Upwind 304 ms, WENO 2278 ms, OCoFE 339/1191 ms) and Runge artefacts in the earlier OCoFE (pp. 5-6); mesh study N_m = 300 (p. 5); 228 weight vectors, K = 512 Pareto cloud with non-convergence read from mixed-colour clusters (p. 6); 25,920 SLSQP runs (~3 h on 72 cores) per weight vector (p. 7); two verified Pareto policies, S_f saturates, Lambda ratios reported (p. 7).
positioning: Extends Henson and Zhang-Henson controller studies and corrects Zhu et al.'s OCoFE numerics; Miettinen for multiobjective methods; lists MPC options for future work (pp. 2, 4-5, 8).
writing: Limitations written into the results paragraph (may not converge to true Pareto points; rough heuristics), hedged practical implications (pp. 6-7).
limits_future: Weighted sum finds only convex parts of the front (p. 5); no global optimality (p. 6); model-plant mismatch (p. 7); expensive MPC; choice of MPC scheme left as an open question (p. 8).

method_links.note: Numerics read before optimizing: discretization schemes compared for positivity and dispersion, past Runge artefacts diagnosed, nondimensionalization; weak evidence because the voice is mainly the Braatz group's.
Non-convergence of the Pareto cloud reported, costs stated, claims hedged; but the delta study and epsilon-constraint verification are not shown.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: coarse-to-fine continuation in the control discretization
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Warm-start the 2K-element problem from the bisected K-element optimum, K = 2 to 512/1024; parallels mesh refinement on demand in S091 (pp. 24-25, 31).

transferable: Run an open-loop discretization shoot-out (accuracy, positivity, diffusion, dispersion, median wall time) and a mesh study before optimizing a PDE-constrained model (pp. 5-6).
Warm-start high-resolution control parameterizations by bisecting converged coarse trajectories and multistart with Gaussian perturbations of decreasing variance (pp. 5-7).
Treat clusters where different weights map to the same objective point as a symptom of local (non-Pareto) solutions and verify selected points with the epsilon-constraint method (pp. 6-7).
Summarize Pareto tradeoffs between two verified policies by ratios of objective differences (eq. (26), p. 7).
coauthors: Krystian Ganko (first), Marc D. Berliner, Jinwook Rhyu, Liang Wu, Richard D. Braatz

quotes.text: The weighting method only uncovers convex portions of the Pareto optimal set.
All discussions above are predicated upon a near-perfect model description of the yeast continuous manufacturing process.
